title: A on Mach 10 Hypersonic Travel and Global Connectivity

transcript.text: Camera action. Sound speed.

transcript.text: Camera action.

transcript.text: What? Camera speed. Camera action. Sound speed.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
transcript.text: Okay, sorry.

transcript.speaker: possible
transcript.text: One of the biggest pushback we get in this idea is that Mach 10 is too fast. Like, you don't have time to take off, accelerate to get to the other places. So people say, why not Mach 4, Mach 3, Mach 2? You know, which are good questions. Also, there's a little bit of, hey, I know this is possible, it makes sense in the physics, but it sounds so far out there that it's scary. Are you sure this can be done? I think those are the two biggest pushbacks. But when you look at the technical aspect there's strong consensus that this can be done. Now the question is Mach 3, Mach 7, 100 passengers, 50 passengers, hydrogen, jet fuel, but not that this is not doable.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
transcript.text: Is there competition to do this?

transcript.speaker: possible
transcript.text: There's a lot of companies working on hypersonics now. There's a bunch of them working on defense applications. We are steering clear of defense and working on civil applications. And there's a few that are trying to build a combined cycle engine, basically an engine that can take you from the ground to hypersonic. Our approach is to skip that engine, use off-the-shelf components. It's going to be less efficient, but we can get sooner to the market. Our idea is to build off the shelf, be an integrator, not a component builder. So all these players could be our suppliers in the future.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
transcript.text: Okay, talk to me about what the world looks like when you have 50 of your planes in the market. And at a reasonable cost, someone can book a supersonic flight from Miami to Japan and get there in 2 hours. What changes about the world?

transcript.speaker: possible
transcript.text: One thing that excites me about this idea is how the world will change when we actually have the second or third generation aircraft on the market. Think about this: you're in San Francisco, You go to the airport, 2 hours later you're in Japan, you have the best sushi in the world, 2 hours later you fly back home, you are back in time to pick up your kids from school. So now the world is no longer a big place. Anywhere in the world is under commuter distance at a fair price, not hundreds of thousands of dollars but a couple of thousands on the ticket. So people today live in San Francisco and commute often to LA. Think about that anywhere in the world. If I want to go skiing Truckee from San Francisco, it's 4 hours. It's gonna be faster for me to fly to Japan, to fly to Switzerland. Now, why should I have a ski lease in the mountains here when I can have them in the Alps, which I maybe like more or less, right? How many times do you skip the wedding of your best friend in the Philippines, Malaysia, or any Australia faraway place because it's too far, I don't have enough time, I have important meeting. Not anymore. Fly there, have the wedding, and be back in home before your hangover is over. It's like amazing how the world collapsed to a 2 to 3 hours point to point.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
transcript.text: I see this having like a tremendous impact on families. Like, I was in an unfortunate situation where I got a phone call, my grandfather was in the hospital and it— and his condition did not look good. And thankfully somebody, you know, like, that I was with insisted on taking me to the airport and making sure I got on the plane. And I arrived just in time to have this conversation with my grandfather that wouldn't have happened had that not happened. And I'm lucky that I was only a 1-hour flight away from him. What is the impact on families maybe who are traveling, but maybe, you know, like, what does this open up for people who maybe want to live somewhere else? Like, I, you know, I love Australia. One of my best friends live there. One of the reasons I don't ever consider living there is because that's just too far away from my family. What is the impact on families when no city is more than 2 hours away from another?

transcript.speaker: possible
transcript.text: One big motivation on this idea for me, it's my family. I'm originally from Argentina. I live in San Francisco. That's 16 hours flight. My brother with my niece lives in London. That's like 12 hours away. And my older brother is in Australia, which is like 20 hours by plane from here. So there's birthdays, when they were born, spending time with them, going to school, are things that I'm missing. And going and visit them is like 16-hour flight plus 10 hours change zone, so it's like 24 hours one way, 24 hours coming back. It's impossible for me to visit them often. With this on the market, I can go every weekend. One weekend to Australia, visit my niece. Another weekend to Argentina, be with my nephew. Another weekend in London. And the that allows me to not have to worry how far I am from my family when I decide where I want to live. Last year, unfortunately, my dad passed away, and I was lucky enough, by some coincidence, I was in Argentina. Unfortunately, my brothers were not there. So the doctor was like, hey, your dad is not gonna make it to tomorrow. What should we do? I have brothers in Australia, in London, in, uh, other parts of Europe that they couldn't say goodbye. There was no way physically for them to make it there, whether we needed 30 hours to reach our small town, and they couldn't say goodbye to my father. So those things will no longer happen. You're going to be able last minute get there, say your goodbyes. So that's very personal reason to work on this.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
transcript.text: What will it mean to you personally when thousands and thousands of people are having a different experience than what your brother's experienced and are able to make it to these important moments? What will it mean to you personally when that is normal for thousands of people?

transcript.speaker: possible
transcript.text: I think when I think about the future and how people will experience life differently because the great work the team is doing, it makes me feel like this is worth it, right? Sure, getting, building something fun is worth it. Maybe if you make a shit ton of money as well, but the positive impact on the world, to have the family together, to not miss your dad's funeral, to not miss baptisms, to not miss weddings, Because being from Latin America, family for me is very important. And I think this is a kind of impact that I would be very glad to have on the world.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
transcript.text: What are some downsides to this level of connectivity and mobility?

transcript.speaker: possible
transcript.text: I think one of the things I'm not so sure about is the downside. It's— there's one, the things you don't know. That you don't know, how people will adapt this, how we start using it. And also what happens when thousands of people from San Francisco decide to have a summer house in the middle of Patagonia because now they can. How that will affect the locals, right? How will it be negative, that influx of money or influence of cash? I don't know. I think there's potential there for gentrification worldwide. But I think that there's less people with so much money, so I think it's gonna even out good. But that's a potential negative.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
transcript.text: How do you think countries will need to respond to the bureaucracy that it currently takes for certain types of travel when now I can just— I can go to a business meeting in Japan in person You know, certain— like, that might not require a visa right now for an American, but how do countries— how are they, how are they going to need to adapt when I can get a call and I, and I want to go somewhere in 2 hours?

transcript.speaker: possible
transcript.text: One thing I'm thinking about also, it's how bureaucracy will need to change. I cannot spend 3 hours doing immigration clearance. I cannot spend months waiting for a visa when I can just get a phone call, need to fly to Australia for a meeting and come back, right? So I think we are moving more into integration, less barriers, enabling more frequent and easy moving around, especially for short-time visits. Now nobody will think going to Australia for a weekend from Argentina, that's 30 hours of flight, but with this new technology that would be possible. So I think there's a need for adapting and looking on how that could be possible.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
transcript.text: What do you think the impact of your technology will be on what I would call digital nomadism and long-term travel and people who live a very borderless global life?

transcript.speaker: possible
transcript.text: I think one of the questions here for me is what happens with remote work. I used to be nomad and remote And the way I did that was staying in a small place and moving around near there. So I was in Europe, moving around Europe, and maybe working with the US. Now with this, I think I can decide where to live and where to work independently of anything else. Independently of infrastructure, or independently of healthcare, or independently of school or family. I could have my weekend home in the middle of the mountains with no access to services, work in San Francisco and having my healthcare plan in Argentina. Now what you do with neighborhoods, what you do with cities, can be do global, which it's kind of mind-blowing.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
transcript.text: Is there a component of what this unlocks that has to do with emergency response, or like catastrophe sort of response or things like that? Or, you know, you're looking at this as more of like a passenger commercial thing, but, you know, the ability to get from one place to Japan in 2 hours could have some other very important implications, right?

transcript.speaker: possible
transcript.text: Like— So one of the other things to think about this problem is how fast cargo transport change and what does it mean. So if you are waiting for an organ, you have to leave 30 minutes away from the recipient to be able to be on the list. Now with this airplane, that's not a few miles, this is almost half the world, right? When there's an emergency, you need to deploy something urgently instead of having to think, oh, it's going to take 24 hours to get there, it's 1 or 2 hours. If you look at supply chain, supply chain, if you have a factory and your machine is down and you're losing $1, $2, $3 million an hour of products that you're not churning, having the spare part flown in halfway from the world, saving you 25 hours. Now it changed completely the way you, how you think about critical components for your supply chain, your stocks. It kind of impacts completely the entire way we think about lag times, delays. You can buy, if you want now, you can buy bread from France, fly to United States, and it will be warm when it arrives. So everything changed completely. You can buy ice cream from Argentina and have it in Africa if that's what you want.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
transcript.text: I want some pistachio gelato from Rome immediately.

transcript.speaker: possible
